newsitem.title: USA: Russia aid increase questioned in Senate.
newsitem.headline: Russia aid increase questioned in Senate.

text.p: A key senator on Thursday questioned the Clinton administration's proposal to sharply increase aid to Russia while holding down assistance to most other former Soviet states.
The administration requested $900 million in aid for 12 former Soviet states for the year starting Oct. 1, up from $625 million this year. Total aid to Russia accounts for $246 million.

"This request continues to reflect a bias towards Moscow at the expense of our deep interests in the region and fails to recognise we can't buy our way out of the economic crisis which cripples opportunity in Russia," said Sen. Mitch McConnell, a Kentucky Republican.
McConnell spoke at a meeting of his Appropriations subcommittee that handles foreign aid funding, as he heard testimony from Brian Atwood, administrator of the Agency for International Development.
AID's budget request of $7.2 billion for its worldwide aid programme sought to reverse a decline in foreign aid over several years and represented a $476 million increase over the current level.
McConnell applauded the administration's increased foreign affairs budget after years of cuts that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright described as "unilateral diplomatic disarmament."
But other members of Congress said it will be difficult to win approval of the increase while other important domestic programmes were being cut.

Sen. Chuck Hagel, a newly elected Republican from Nebraska who chairs the Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee that deals with foreign aid, told Atwood on Wednesday he was not convinced all funds for international programmes were being spent effectively and efficiently.

McConnell's counterpart in the House, Alabama Republican Representative Sonny Callahan, told Albright two weeks ago that given the effort to balance the federal budget in five years, the subcommittee was unlikely to get all the funds needed to meet her priorities.
"Even if such an allocation were available, I'm not sure a 10 percent increase in foreign aid would pass the House," he said.
McConnell, who pushed for high aid levels to Ukraine, complained that this former Soviet state was getting about the same as this year while Russian aid was being boosted.
AID sought $241 million for Russia in 1998 compared to $95 million this year. Additional Peace Corps spending and Pentagon aid would bring the total to more than $246 million.
The administration sees Ukraine lagging behind Russia in its struggle to privatise its economy and has a stake in Russia's remaining on the reform path.

President Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin conferred by telephone on Thursday and agreed on an agenda for their summit next month that includes efforts to improve Russia's economy, a White House spokesman said.
